nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name:  Carcharhinus leucas
Common Name:  Bull shark

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Chondrichthyes
	Order:		Elasmobranchii
	Family:	Carcharhinidae

Other Common Names: Cub shark (52 1360), ground shark (52)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Primarily caught on longlines set for other commercial fishes (tuna, swordfish)(99 791 866); will take almost any bait, but prefers shark or ray.  Flesh is edible and is sold fresh, fresh frozen and smoked (866), but primarily used for fish meal (791 866).  The hide is of good quality and is used for leather (101 791 866).  Fins are used for shark fin soup, and the liver for oil which is extracted for vitamins, particularly vitamin A (791 866).

Recreational:  A popular game fish particularly in the southeast Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico, and off South Africa (866).  The majority of sharks caught are released or discarded, with some being used as mounted trophies or food at home.  In the Gulf of Mexico, bull sharks comprise 7 % of the shark species by number and 11.4 % by weight caught by recreational fishermen (99).  Caught with rod and reel (866).

Ecological Role:  Sharks are considered as apex predators (99).  Bull sharks represent the top carnivore in many estuarine systems.

Indicator:  Sharks, as apex predators, are occasionally monitored and utilized in modeling bioaccumulation of toxic substances in the environment.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body: Overall:  Primarily a coastal species, it is cosmopolitan in tropical-subtropical areas with extensions into some temperate regions (101 788 791 866).  In the western Atlantic, it extends from Massachusetts to southern Brazil (228 788 791 891 1360).  Most abundant in Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean areas (52 101 228 791).  Penetrates far up warm rivers and into freshwater lakes (726 788 790 791 866).  Reported as far up the Mississippi River as Alton, Illinois (726).  Seldom seen offshore (788).

nodes.title: Florida
nodes.body:
One of the most common large sharks in nearshore coastal waters of Florida (660 661).  Commonly caught in the Tampa Bay area (664), and reported as the most abundant shark species in the Indian River Lagoon (660 661).  Also reported as the most common shark off Sarasota (123).  Found in freshwater rivers on the Florida west coast (790).  Small bull sharks are common throughout the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) and are probably using the lagoon as a nursery (997).  Snelson (997) and Gilmore (1272) reported bull sharks to be the most common shark in the IRL.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Bull sharks are nektonic.  They are found from the nearshore marine zone to freshwater rivers (52 101).

Movements and Migrations
Movements of adult female sharks to estuarine nursery areas are for parturition (866).  Young remain in these inshore nursery areas, but juveniles and adults move to deeper coastal waters (866).  Other movements are probably associated with changing temperatures.  In the western Atlantic, a north and south migration coinciding with spring and fall occurs along the US east coast (666 866).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Coastal, estuarine, riverine and lacustrine environments.  Usually found close inshore in waters <30m deep (52 866).  Commonly found in bays, lagoons, tidal passes, river mouths, near wharves, and just off the surf line (52 101 866).  Often ascend rivers for long distances (52 101 251 726 790 958 1037).

Substrate:  Considered a bottom-living species (791), it is often found in muddy areas with few other shark competitors (866).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature:  Snelson (660) collected juvenile bull shark in the Indian River Lagoon system of Florida at temperatures ranging from 20.0_32.0 C and reported two individuals that succumbed to hypothermal stress around a temperature of 8.0 C, during January.  Additionally, Gilmore et al. (236) reports bull sharks as rarely killed in freezes in the Indian River Lagoon. Bull sharks were not captured during the winter in Indian River Lagoon, but it was suggested that this absence reflects depressed activity caused by low water temperatures (10_15 C) rather than emigration from the lagoon (661).  Bull shark sightings do occur during the winter at some of the heated discharge canals associated with power plants (Steve Traxler).  Branstetter (per. comm.) suggested that water temperatures must be at least 18 C before bull sharks advance into the estuaries.  Thomerson (726) suggested water temperature as the limiting factor for the advancement of C. leucas up the Mississippi River.  Only when temperatures are >24 C particularly during the summer and fall do the sharks move up the Mississippi River (726).

Salinity:  Occurs in brackish or freshwater, mainly as pups and juveniles but also as adult females (52 101 866).  This occurrence may be related to inshore migrations of the females for parturition (228 661).  After birth, the juveniles often spend considerable time in these brackish waters (228).  Branstetter (64) noted that these sharks are concentrated around freshwater inflows, or at least the fishery for them is.  One study reported the collection of juveniles from a salinity range of 1.6 to 2.3 ppt (374).  Collected in salinities ranging from 18 to 42 ppt in the Indian River Lagoon (660), and in freshwater rivers of southwest Florida (790 1043).  Newborns have been taken at salinities of 0.8 ppt in Shark River, Florida (D. Wright and T. Kranzer pers. comm., cited in Loftus and Kushlan [790]).  Thomerson (726) reported that C. leucas is the only shark known to be able to deal with the osmotic demands of either fresh water or sea water for periods of at least months and probably years.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  Fertilization is internal.  Viviparous with a yolk-sac placenta (866).

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
In the northern Gulf of Mexico, gravid females are caught in July and August, with pups being born in April and May suggesting a gestation period of 10 - 11 months (62).  Data collected from bull sharks collected at Sarasota indicate that mating takes place in June and July in the Gulf of Mexico, with pups being born in April, May and June (123).  Gestation probably lasts 10 - 11 months (62 101 123 866).  Females move into brackish water estuaries to give birth and the young utilize these areas as nurseries (62 88 123 661 791 1356 1359).

Fecundity: The number of pups per litter ranges from 1 to 13 (791 866).  Snelson et al. (661) took a 249 cm TL female with 12 near term embryos.  Most other investigators report litters of 4 - 5 (52 123).  Females apparently do not bear young every year (123 661).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Embryos:  Development is viviparous _ embryos initially dependent on stored yolk but are later nourished by mother through a placental connection.  Dodrill (184) proposed that during uterine development one or more pups may develop to extraordinary size at the expense of other litter mates.

Juvenile:  Size at birth ranges from 56_81 cm TL (62 63 64 101 661 866) and averages around 75 cm TL (101 661).  Caillouet et al. (88) showed no significant differences in lengths or weights between male and female neonates shortly after birth.  They (88) presented the following length-weight relationships:
[eq]
        Males:  Log W = 2.90(Log L) - 4.96     r^2 = 0.82
        Females:  Log W = 3.06(Log L) - 5.26     r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]
where W = weight in grams and L = length in cm.

The juvenile weights increase rapidly as maturity approaches (62).  Branstetter and Stiles (63) estimated growth rates of 15 - 20 cm/yr for the first five years, 10 cm/yr for 6 - 10 year old sharks, 5 - 7 cm/yr for 11 - 16 year old sharks, and less than 4 - 5 cm/yr for sharks older than 16 years.

Adult:  Smallest mature male reported as 212 cm TL; smallest female was 228 cm TL (62).  Males mature at 210_220 cm TL or 14_15 years of age; females mature at >225 cm TL or over 18 years of age (63).  In Florida, bull sharks begin to mature at 200_215 cm TL (666) and the smallest reported males and females are 225 and 233 cm TL, respectively (123).  Females grow larger than males (64 123).  Adult size reported as 225_300 cm TL (males) and 233_300 cm TL (females) (1037), reported to grow as large as 350 cm (788).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Reported stomach contents have contained squid (Loligo sp.) and fishes (Stenotomus caprinus, Diplectrum formosum, Anchoa hepsetus, and Brevoortia spp.)(62). Jaws commonly contain spines from rays (62).  Other bony fishes reported from the stomachs of bull sharks are: Archosargus probatocephalus, Caranx sp., Centropomus undecimalis, Euthynnus alleteratus, Arius felis, Lactophrys tricornis, Megalops atlanticus, Mugil sp. (123); Anguilla rostrata, Roccus americanus, and Micropogonias undulatus (631). Castro (101) noted that bull sharks feed on other sharks, preying heavily on small sandbar sharks, rays, bony fishes, molluscs, and crustaceans.  Incidents of cannibalism were �provoked� by Vorenberg (1358), but have also been reported from bull sharks captured in the wild (661).  Snelson et al (661) suggest that catfishes (Arius felis, Bagre marinus) and stingrays (Dasyatis sabina, D. sayi) are very important food items in the diet of bull sharks.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Bull sharks are a top carnivore with slow growth and relatively low reproductive capacity.  Because of these factors only a limited commercial and sport fishery for these sharks can be sustained.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Scientific Name:  Carcharhinus leucas
Common Name:  Bull shark

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:		Chondrichthyes
	Order:		Elasmobranchii
	Family:	Carcharhinidae

Other Common Names: Cub shark (52 1360), ground shark (52)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Primarily caught on longlines set for other commercial fishes (tuna, swordfish)(99 791 866); will take almost any bait, but prefers shark or ray.  Flesh is edible and is sold fresh, fresh frozen and smoked (866), but primarily used for fish meal (791 866).  The hide is of good quality and is used for leather (101 791 866).  Fins are used for shark fin soup, and the liver for oil which is extracted for vitamins, particularly vitamin A (791 866).

Recreational:  A popular game fish particularly in the southeast Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico, and off South Africa (866).  The majority of sharks caught are released or discarded, with some being used as mounted trophies or food at home.  In the Gulf of Mexico, bull sharks comprise 7 % of the shark species by number and 11.4 % by weight caught by recreational fishermen (99).  Caught with rod and reel (866).

Ecological Role:  Sharks are considered as apex predators (99).  Bull sharks represent the top carnivore in many estuarine systems.

Indicator:  Sharks, as apex predators, are occasionally monitored and utilized in modeling bioaccumulation of toxic substances in the environment.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content: Overall:  Primarily a coastal species, it is cosmopolitan in tropical-subtropical areas with extensions into some temperate regions (101 788 791 866).  In the western Atlantic, it extends from Massachusetts to southern Brazil (228 788 791 891 1360).  Most abundant in Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean areas (52 101 228 791).  Penetrates far up warm rivers and into freshwater lakes (726 788 790 791 866).  Reported as far up the Mississippi River as Alton, Illinois (726).  Seldom seen offshore (788).

sections.heading: Florida
sections.content:
One of the most common large sharks in nearshore coastal waters of Florida (660 661).  Commonly caught in the Tampa Bay area (664), and reported as the most abundant shark species in the Indian River Lagoon (660 661).  Also reported as the most common shark off Sarasota (123).  Found in freshwater rivers on the Florida west coast (790).  Small bull sharks are common throughout the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) and are probably using the lagoon as a nursery (997).  Snelson (997) and Gilmore (1272) reported bull sharks to be the most common shark in the IRL.

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Bull sharks are nektonic.  They are found from the nearshore marine zone to freshwater rivers (52 101).

Movements and Migrations
Movements of adult female sharks to estuarine nursery areas are for parturition (866).  Young remain in these inshore nursery areas, but juveniles and adults move to deeper coastal waters (866).  Other movements are probably associated with changing temperatures.  In the western Atlantic, a north and south migration coinciding with spring and fall occurs along the US east coast (666 866).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Coastal, estuarine, riverine and lacustrine environments.  Usually found close inshore in waters <30m deep (52 866).  Commonly found in bays, lagoons, tidal passes, river mouths, near wharves, and just off the surf line (52 101 866).  Often ascend rivers for long distances (52 101 251 726 790 958 1037).

Substrate:  Considered a bottom-living species (791), it is often found in muddy areas with few other shark competitors (866).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Temperature:  Snelson (660) collected juvenile bull shark in the Indian River Lagoon system of Florida at temperatures ranging from 20.0_32.0 C and reported two individuals that succumbed to hypothermal stress around a temperature of 8.0 C, during January.  Additionally, Gilmore et al. (236) reports bull sharks as rarely killed in freezes in the Indian River Lagoon. Bull sharks were not captured during the winter in Indian River Lagoon, but it was suggested that this absence reflects depressed activity caused by low water temperatures (10_15 C) rather than emigration from the lagoon (661).  Bull shark sightings do occur during the winter at some of the heated discharge canals associated with power plants (Steve Traxler).  Branstetter (per. comm.) suggested that water temperatures must be at least 18 C before bull sharks advance into the estuaries.  Thomerson (726) suggested water temperature as the limiting factor for the advancement of C. leucas up the Mississippi River.  Only when temperatures are >24 C particularly during the summer and fall do the sharks move up the Mississippi River (726).

Salinity:  Occurs in brackish or freshwater, mainly as pups and juveniles but also as adult females (52 101 866).  This occurrence may be related to inshore migrations of the females for parturition (228 661).  After birth, the juveniles often spend considerable time in these brackish waters (228).  Branstetter (64) noted that these sharks are concentrated around freshwater inflows, or at least the fishery for them is.  One study reported the collection of juveniles from a salinity range of 1.6 to 2.3 ppt (374).  Collected in salinities ranging from 18 to 42 ppt in the Indian River Lagoon (660), and in freshwater rivers of southwest Florida (790 1043).  Newborns have been taken at salinities of 0.8 ppt in Shark River, Florida (D. Wright and T. Kranzer pers. comm., cited in Loftus and Kushlan [790]).  Thomerson (726) reported that C. leucas is the only shark known to be able to deal with the osmotic demands of either fresh water or sea water for periods of at least months and probably years.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode:  Fertilization is internal.  Viviparous with a yolk-sac placenta (866).

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
In the northern Gulf of Mexico, gravid females are caught in July and August, with pups being born in April and May suggesting a gestation period of 10 - 11 months (62).  Data collected from bull sharks collected at Sarasota indicate that mating takes place in June and July in the Gulf of Mexico, with pups being born in April, May and June (123).  Gestation probably lasts 10 - 11 months (62 101 123 866).  Females move into brackish water estuaries to give birth and the young utilize these areas as nurseries (62 88 123 661 791 1356 1359).

Fecundity: The number of pups per litter ranges from 1 to 13 (791 866).  Snelson et al. (661) took a 249 cm TL female with 12 near term embryos.  Most other investigators report litters of 4 - 5 (52 123).  Females apparently do not bear young every year (123 661).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Embryos:  Development is viviparous _ embryos initially dependent on stored yolk but are later nourished by mother through a placental connection.  Dodrill (184) proposed that during uterine development one or more pups may develop to extraordinary size at the expense of other litter mates.

Juvenile:  Size at birth ranges from 56_81 cm TL (62 63 64 101 661 866) and averages around 75 cm TL (101 661).  Caillouet et al. (88) showed no significant differences in lengths or weights between male and female neonates shortly after birth.  They (88) presented the following length-weight relationships:
[eq]
        Males:  Log W = 2.90(Log L) - 4.96     r^2 = 0.82
        Females:  Log W = 3.06(Log L) - 5.26     r^2 = 0.98
[/eq]
where W = weight in grams and L = length in cm.

The juvenile weights increase rapidly as maturity approaches (62).  Branstetter and Stiles (63) estimated growth rates of 15 - 20 cm/yr for the first five years, 10 cm/yr for 6 - 10 year old sharks, 5 - 7 cm/yr for 11 - 16 year old sharks, and less than 4 - 5 cm/yr for sharks older than 16 years.

Adult:  Smallest mature male reported as 212 cm TL; smallest female was 228 cm TL (62).  Males mature at 210_220 cm TL or 14_15 years of age; females mature at >225 cm TL or over 18 years of age (63).  In Florida, bull sharks begin to mature at 200_215 cm TL (666) and the smallest reported males and females are 225 and 233 cm TL, respectively (123).  Females grow larger than males (64 123).  Adult size reported as 225_300 cm TL (males) and 233_300 cm TL (females) (1037), reported to grow as large as 350 cm (788).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Reported stomach contents have contained squid (Loligo sp.) and fishes (Stenotomus caprinus, Diplectrum formosum, Anchoa hepsetus, and Brevoortia spp.)(62). Jaws commonly contain spines from rays (62).  Other bony fishes reported from the stomachs of bull sharks are: Archosargus probatocephalus, Caranx sp., Centropomus undecimalis, Euthynnus alleteratus, Arius felis, Lactophrys tricornis, Megalops atlanticus, Mugil sp. (123); Anguilla rostrata, Roccus americanus, and Micropogonias undulatus (631). Castro (101) noted that bull sharks feed on other sharks, preying heavily on small sandbar sharks, rays, bony fishes, molluscs, and crustaceans.  Incidents of cannibalism were �provoked� by Vorenberg (1358), but have also been reported from bull sharks captured in the wild (661).  Snelson et al (661) suggest that catfishes (Arius felis, Bagre marinus) and stingrays (Dasyatis sabina, D. sayi) are very important food items in the diet of bull sharks.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Bull sharks are a top carnivore with slow growth and relatively low reproductive capacity.  Because of these factors only a limited commercial and sport fishery for these sharks can be sustained.
